### Tutorial 7.1: Building a Revenue Forecasting Model from Charles River Sales Data

**Context and objective.** You will aggregate Charles River sales invoice data into monthly revenue totals, run a regression analysis using month number as the independent variable, and use the resulting model to forecast revenue for the next quarter. This exercise simulates the kind of revenue projection that a financial analyst might prepare for management or that an auditor might use to set expectations for a substantive analytical procedure.

**Prerequisites.** Open the Charles River dataset in Excel. You need the merged InvoiceLines dataset that includes InvoiceDate and LineTotal for each invoice line, as prepared in Chapter 5. If you completed Tutorial 5.3 or Tutorial 6.2, your workbook already contains this data. The Data Analysis ToolPak must be enabled (see instructions above).

**Step 1.** Create a new worksheet and name it "MonthlyRevenue." You will aggregate the invoice lines into monthly totals. In cell A1, type "Monthly Revenue Summary" as a title. In cell A3, type "Month" and in cell B3, type "MonthNumber." In cell C3, type "Revenue."

**Step 2.** Determine the range of months in the Charles River data. The sales invoices span a 24-month period from January 2023 through December 2024. List each month in column A, starting with "Jan-2023" in cell A4 and continuing through "Dec-2024" in cell A27. This gives you 24 months of data. In column B, number the months sequentially from 1 (for Jan-2023) through 24 (for Dec-2024). The MonthNumber column serves as the independent variable in the regression because it converts a time sequence into a numeric predictor.

**Step 3.** In cell C4, use a SUMIFS formula to calculate the total revenue for January 2023. If your merged dataset table is named "InvoiceLines" and includes an InvoiceDate column, the formula is =SUMIFS(InvoiceLines[LineTotal], InvoiceLines[InvoiceDate], ">="&DATE(2023,1,1), InvoiceLines[InvoiceDate], "<"&DATE(2023,2,1)). This sums the billed amount for all invoice lines with an InvoiceDate in January 2023.

**Step 4.** Copy the formula in C4 down through C27, adjusting the year and month parameters for each row. Alternatively, if you added Year and Month columns during data preparation, you can use simpler SUMIFS criteria referencing those columns directly. Verify that the sum of all monthly values equals the grand total of LineTotal in your source data.

**Step 5.** Before running the regression, examine the data visually. Select the MonthNumber and Revenue columns and insert a scatter chart (Insert tab, Chart group, Scatter). The chart should show monthly revenue on the vertical axis and month number on the horizontal axis. Look for a general upward or downward trend, any obvious outliers, and whether the relationship appears approximately linear. If the data shows a clear curve, a linear regression may not be the best approach.

*[Figure 7.5: Scatter chart of Charles River monthly revenue versus month number. Revenue appears on the vertical axis and month number on the horizontal axis. A general upward trend is visible, though individual months show variation around the trend line.]*

**Step 6.** Run the regression. Go to the Data tab, click Data Analysis, and select Regression. In the dialog box, set the Input Y Range to the Revenue column (C3:C27, including the label). Set the Input X Range to the MonthNumber column (B3:B27, including the label). Check the "Labels" box. Under Output options, select "New Worksheet Ply" and type "RegressionOutput" as the sheet name. Check the "Residuals" and "Residual Plots" boxes. Click OK.

**Step 7.** Examine the regression output. Locate the R Square value in the Regression Statistics section. This tells you what proportion of the monthly variation in revenue is explained by the linear time trend. Locate the Coefficients section and note the Intercept and the slope for MonthNumber. The intercept is the model's estimate of revenue in "month zero" (the month before the data begins), and the slope is the estimated amount by which revenue changes each month. Check the p-value for the MonthNumber coefficient. If it is below 0.05, the time trend is statistically significant.

**Step 8.** Write the prediction equation. If the intercept is approximately 385,000 and the slope is approximately 9,500, the equation is: Predicted Revenue = 385,000 + 9,500 times MonthNumber. To forecast revenue for the next three months (months 25, 26, and 27), substitute each month number into the equation. On a new worksheet named "Forecast," create a table with columns for MonthNumber, Month Label (Jan-2025, Feb-2025, Mar-2025), Predicted Revenue, and a column for Notes where you will document assumptions.

**Step 9.** Calculate the predicted revenue for each forecast month. For month 25, the predicted revenue is =385000 + 9500 * 25 (use your actual intercept and slope values, not these examples). Record the prediction for each month. In the Notes column, write the key assumption: "This forecast assumes that the linear trend observed over the 24-month historical period will continue at the same rate."

**Step 10.** Examine the residuals. Return to the RegressionOutput worksheet and look at the Residuals section, which shows the difference between the actual revenue and the predicted revenue for each month. Large residuals indicate months where the model was a poor fit. Also look at the Residual Plot, which graphs the residuals against the month number. If the residuals show a random scatter around zero, the linear model is appropriate. If the residuals show a pattern (such as a curve or increasing spread), the linear model may be missing an important feature of the data.

*[Figure 7.6: The regression output worksheet showing the three standard sections (Regression Statistics, ANOVA, Coefficients) and the Residual Plot. Annotations highlight the R Square value, the slope and intercept, and the pattern of residuals in the plot.]*

**Checkpoint.** Your workbook should now contain four worksheets related to this analysis: MonthlyRevenue (the aggregated data), a scatter chart (either embedded or on its own sheet), RegressionOutput (the full regression results), and Forecast (the three-month projection). The R Square value should be positive and ideally above 0.50, indicating that at least half the monthly variation in revenue is explained by the time trend. The slope should be positive, indicating that revenue tends to increase over time. The forecast values should be reasonable extensions of the historical trend, not dramatically different from recent months.

> **[WATCH OUT]**
> Regression-based forecasts assume that the historical pattern will continue unchanged into the future. This assumption is often reasonable for short-term projections (one to three periods ahead) but becomes increasingly risky for longer horizons. In accounting, auditors and analysts typically limit regression-based forecasts to one or two periods beyond the historical data unless there is strong reason to believe the trend is driven by stable underlying factors. Always state the time horizon and the key assumptions when presenting a regression-based forecast.
